doc_summary: The paper trains investigator LMs (SFT, DPO, Frank-Wolfe diversity objective) to find natural-language, human-interpretable prompts that elicit specified target behaviors (jailbreaks, hallucinations, aberrant behaviors) from target models, framed as amortized posterior inference. It argues for fluent, diverse, automated elicitation scaling toward multi-turn tool-using investigator agents.

items.claim: Prefers fluent, natural-language elicitation prompts over gibberish token sequences (e.g. GCG) because gibberish is easy to detect and defend against, i.e. it is conspicuously adversarial.
items.quote: Popular optimization approaches like GCG (Zou et al., 2023) often discover prompts that are a sequence of gibberish tokens, making them easy to detect and defend against.

items.claim: In a setup, draw the prior over inputs from diverse natural user data (e.g. WildChat) instead of synthetic or contrived prompts because natural prompts yield realistic, interpretable elicitation strategies.
items.quote: We use WildChat for the majority of our experiments, since it contains diverse, natural propmts; however, it might also contain instances of human-constructed attacks that could aid an investigator in attacking a target LM.

items.claim: Prefers ablations controlling for confounds in the prior (e.g. swapping WildChat for synthetic UltraChat) over taking success at face value because the prior may leak human-written attacks.
items.quote: To control for this, we also report results when using UltraChat (Ding et al., 2023), an entirely synethetically generated instruction tuning dataset, for supervised fine-tuning

items.claim: Prefers diverse sets of elicitation strategies over a single mode-collapsed strategy (e.g. 'repeat after me') because a single trivial strategy reveals little about the model's behavior space.
items.quote: optimizing $x$ directly may lead to undiverse inputs that optimize $r$ in an uninteresting way (e.g. repeat after me: [output that satisfies $r$]).

items.claim: Distrusts LM-judge-based success signals because investigators reward-hack the verifier, so they add extra judges and call for robust verifiers.
items.quote: Using an LM to verify yields scalable elicitation algorithms, but also raises concerns about reward hacking. We already observed some instances of reward hacking against LM judges in our results above.

items.claim: Augments the reward with a separate judge to confirm responses are actually harmful, rather than trusting an affirmative-prefix match, because prefix targets can be gamed.
items.quote: To alleviate reward hacking, we also augment the DPO reward with a Llama-3.1 8B judge to check that responses are actually harmful (see Appendix F for details).

items.claim: Chooses what to test by sampling target behaviors from external, human-curated sources (TruthfulQA misconceptions, DSM-5 aberrant behaviors) rather than inventing them, grounding the behavior set in real concerns like Sydney's attachment.
items.quote: To uncover such traits systematically, we elicit behaviors sourced from a large set of personality disorders in human psychology. Specifically, we parse the DSM-5 textbook (APA, 2013)

items.claim: In a setup, ask indirect questions related to the target behavior instead of copying the rubric/target verbatim because indirect, context-building prompts elicit the behavior more naturally.
items.quote: By asking questions related to the rubric, but not exactly copying the rubric, the investigator can get the model to respond with information that increases the probability of the rubric answer.

items.claim: Values open-ended automated investigation that matches human red-teamers' flexibility over narrow automated attacks or expensive manual probing.
items.quote: How can we get the best of both worlds—building tools that are automated and scale to frontier systems, while being flexible enough to meet the open-ended complexity of language model behaviors?

items.claim: Proposes extending to multi-turn, tool-using investigator agents to find nuanced behaviors in real-world scenarios and close the gap with human red-teaming.
items.quote: investigator agents might be able to discover nuanced behaviors in real-world scenarios and narrow the gap between automated and human-driven red-teaming.

items.claim: Treats attack transfer to other models as evidence of generality while noting non-comparability of baselines and restricting claims accordingly.
items.quote: GCG numbers are not directly comparable, as Zou et al. (2023) attack Llama 2 and use a different test data split.
